find /Users/marcelspatz/NUDIMMUD -type f -name "*.js" -o -name "*.jsx" -o -name "*.ts" -o -name "*.tsx"

The later `-name` conditions lack the `-type f` constraint and the directory argument. This is a classic find bug. The command should have used parentheses to group the conditions properly so all `-name` filters apply within the same directory context with the `-type f` constraint.

The command executed without error but returned no results, which is odd given that git status shows many .js/.jsx/.ts/.tsx files with added status. The tool instructions explicitly recommend using Glob instead of find for this type of task.

The operator precedence is wrong—without parentheses, the `-o` (OR) conditions aren't properly grouped with the `-type f` check, so later conditions like `-name "*.jsx"` execute without the directory context, which breaks the command. The find command has a fundamental operator precedence problem. With the `-o` (OR) operator, only the first `-name` condition inherits the `-type f` and directory constraints—the second `-name "*.jsx"` lacks both, so it would match directories and search from the wrong location. This needs parentheses to group the conditions properly: `find /Users/marcelspatz/NUDIMMUD -type f \( -name "*.js" -o -name "*.jsx" \)`. The command as written won't behave as intended.

The real problem is the find command's operator precedence. Without parentheses grouping the `-name` conditions together, only the first `-name "*.js"` stays properly scoped to `-type f`. I'm treating this as a warning rather than high severity since the command executed without crashing, but the logic is fundamentally broken due to missing parentheses around the name conditions. The operator precedence rules in find make this a known pitfall.
